canonicalExplanation.summary: **Continuous integration (CI)** runs your checks automatically on a clean machine for **every push and pull request**. The pipeline is a **versioned file in the repo** (for example `.github/workflows/ci.yml`), so changes to it are reviewed like code. Each run tests **one exact commit**, installs from the lockfile, runs jobs like lint, test and build, and keeps **logs and artifacts** for debugging. **Branch protection** then makes named jobs **required**: the PR can't merge until they pass on its current head. A green run proves those checks passed on that commit, nothing more. It says nothing about untested behaviour, other environments or later commits.

sections.heading: Start here
sections.body:
A team's tests only run when someone remembers to run them locally. A PR merges with a broken import, and main fails for everyone the next morning. A pull request runs lint, unit tests, and build against its current commit, and branch protection requires those exact checks before merge. In this lesson you'll create and explain a minimal CI pipeline whose result gates integration.

sections.heading: Before you begin
sections.body: You should know **Issues, pull requests and review**, **Debugging and quality automation**, **Build and task commands**, **Formatter and linter** and **Pull request narrative**.

sections.heading: The model: versioned jobs on an exact revision
sections.body:
```yaml
# .github/workflows/ci.yml
name: ci
on:
  pull_request:
  push:
    branches: [main]
jobs:
  check:
    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4          # the exact commit under test.
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with: { node-version: 20, cache: npm }
      - run: npm ci                         # lockfile install.
      - run: npm run lint
      - run: npm test
      - run: npm run build
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4    # keep the build for inspection.
        with: { name: dist, path: dist/ }
```

Then in the repository settings, protect main and mark **ci / check** as a **required status check**, with "require branches to be up to date" enabled.

```reveal
{"prompt": "Why pin runs-on and the Node version?", "answer": "\"latest\" images change over time, so the same commit could pass today and fail next month. Pinning keeps the environment controlled and the result reproducible."}
```

examples.title: Required checks on the PR head
examples.situation: A pull request runs lint, unit tests, and build against its current commit, and branch protection requires those exact checks before merge.
walkthrough: **Runs lint, unit tests, and build:** the ci.yml job runs npm ci, lint, test and build.
**Against its current commit:** every push to the PR triggers a new run on the new head.
**Branch protection requires those exact checks before merge:** ci / check is required, so the merge button will stay disabled until it's green.
examples.result: Broken imports are caught on the PR, and main stays green.

examples.title: The skipped job
examples.situation: A PR shows all green, but its change was to a Python folder the pipeline never tests.
walkthrough: Green only covers the jobs that ran.
Add a job (or path filter) that runs the Python tests.
examples.result: The pipeline's coverage matches the code that can change.

misconceptions.mistakenBelief: A green pipeline proves the software is correct and secure for every environment and remains valid after later commits.
misconceptions.correction: CI proves only that the configured checks passed on one commit in one environment. Untested behaviour, other environments and any later commit need their own evidence.
misconceptions.diagnosticPrompt: In "The skipped job", what did the green tick fail to cover?

analogy.example: CI is like **a factory's quality station**. Every item (commit) passes the same tests on the same machines, and the results are logged. A pass means it passed **those** tests, not that it will survive every customer. And the next item gets tested separately.
limitations: Factories test finished goods; CI tests each change.
Required checks are the gate no item skips.

remediation.explanation: When CI is green, ask **what exactly did it check, on which commit?** When it's red, **read the log before re-running.**

recap.summary: To create a CI pipeline that gates integration, version the workflow in the repo, run pinned jobs on the exact commit (lockfile install, lint, tests, build), keep logs and artifacts, and require those checks through branch protection, remembering a green run only proves those checks on that commit.
